title: Bhai Nand Lal
hook: a Persian poet and scholar who served at Guru Gobind Singh's court

segments.voice: Yesterday, the kabitts, and your line, small and bright. Which short line did you carry, and did you read it again before sleep? Day seven hundred thirteen.

Bhai Gurdas has been our guide since this year began, writing in Punjabi and in Braj, close to the Gurus who came before. Now the path hands us to a second teller, from a later court and a different language. He's a learned man who writes in Persian, the language Rumi and Hafiz wrote in, and he spends his gift on Guru Gobind Singh. Sikhs know him by a title of respect, and by a pen name. Today: Bhai Nand Lal.
screen: `A SECOND TELLER.` → `A LATER COURT, A NEW LANGUAGE.` → `PERSIAN, FOR THE GURU.`

segments.voice: Bhai Nand Lal was a poet and a scholar who served at the court of Guru Gobind Singh. Bhai is the same title of respect Bhai Gurdas carries: brother. He wrote under a pen name, Goya, in the Persian manner. And what he wrote, he wrote in Persian. Here's the thing to notice. A court in his world was a place of learning and display, and Persian poetry was a high art, with its own rules, its own pictures, its own long tradition of writing about love for the Divine as a lover writes about the beloved. Nand Lal didn't leave any of that behind when he came to the Guru. He didn't decide that a Sikh had to stop being a poet, or stop writing in the language he'd mastered. He turned the whole art toward the Guru. The lover, the beloved, the beloved's face: in his poems, those old Persian pictures point to the One, and to the Guru who shows the way. That tells you something about the Guru's house. Tradition says Guru Gobind Singh gathered poets around him, and Nand Lal is one of the names Sikhs remember. His learning wasn't treated as a distraction from devotion. It became a way of devotion. Over the next few days you'll meet some of his writing: a book about life, his love-poems, and writings on conduct that carry his name. Today, just meet the man. A scholar at court, a poet with a pen name, who brought the best thing he had, his Persian, and laid it at the Guru's feet. Sikh custom lets his poems, with Bhai Gurdas's vars, be sung in kirtan.
screen: `A POET AND SCHOLAR AT COURT.` · `PEN NAME: GOYA.` · `PERSIAN PICTURES, TURNED TO THE ONE.` · `LEARNING AS A WAY OF DEVOTION.` · then, large: `THE POET AT COURT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read a line of poetry in translation. Find one short line from a poem first written in another language. Persian if you can, or any language not your own. Read it once. Then use the sit to stay with it. Notice what the translator had to choose, and what might have gone missing on the way across. Then think of one gift you have, a skill or a craft or a language, and ask what it would look like turned toward something you love. The bell holds the time.
Bhai Nand Lal. A Persian poet and scholar at Guru Gobind Singh's court, who wrote as Goya and turned his art toward the Guru.
Your line: the poet at court. Today, use one skill you're proud of for something you love, not for show. Day seven hundred thirteen.
